## Welcome {#home}

### Lymphatic Filariasis and Kala-azar

**Learning Objectives:**

- Describe the agent, vector, and clinical spectrum of lymphatic filariasis
- Explain nocturnal periodicity and its diagnostic implication
- Outline Mass Drug Administration and India's ELF programme
- Describe the agent, vector, and clinical features of kala-azar
- Outline the National Kala-azar Elimination Programme's target

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
Both diseases in this module are the subject of active,
time-bound Indian elimination programmes — a useful pairing with
polio (Module 4) and leprosy (Module 9) as examples of the vertical,
disease-specific elimination-programme model.
:::

---

## Lymphatic Filariasis: Agent and Pathogenesis {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

**Agent:** *Wuchereria bancrofti* (the large majority of Indian cases);
*Brugia malayi* accounts for a small minority. **Vector:** *Culex*
mosquitoes.

**Pathogenesis:** adult worms lodge in the **lymphatic vessels**,
causing progressive lymphatic damage and dysfunction — the clinical
picture is a direct consequence of this lymphatic obstruction, not of
the microfilariae circulating in blood.

**Nocturnal periodicity:** microfilariae circulate in **peripheral
blood mainly at night**, synchronized with the night-biting habit of
the *Culex* vector — which is why **blood samples for diagnosis are
collected at night**, a rare and distinctive example of a disease's
biology directly dictating sample-collection timing.

---

## Clinical Spectrum {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

- **Asymptomatic microfilaraemia** — the most common state; the
  person carries circulating microfilariae without symptoms, but
  remains a source of transmission to biting mosquitoes
- **Acute adenolymphangitis (ADL)** — recurrent episodes of fever with
  painful, inflamed lymph nodes/vessels
- **Chronic disease** — **lymphoedema and elephantiasis** (massive limb
  swelling from chronic lymphatic obstruction) and **hydrocele** in
  men — the disfiguring, disabling manifestations that give the
  disease its public health significance

**Why this matters for elimination strategy:** because most infected
people are asymptomatic carriers, case-based treatment alone cannot
interrupt transmission — this is exactly why **Mass Drug
Administration** (next slide), not individual treatment, is the
chosen strategy.

---

## Elimination of Lymphatic Filariasis (ELF) {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

- **Mass Drug Administration (MDA)** — annual single-dose
  co-administration of **DEC (diethylcarbamazine) + Albendazole** to
  the **entire at-risk population** in endemic districts, regardless of
  individual infection status — directly addressing the asymptomatic-
  carrier reservoir described above
- **Morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP)** — hygiene-
  based limb care and hydrocele surgery for those with established
  chronic disease, since MDA prevents new infection but does not
  reverse existing lymphoedema
- **Target:** India's Elimination of Lymphatic Filariasis (ELF)
  programme aims for elimination as a public health problem, verified
  by sustained microfilaria rates below threshold after repeated MDA
  rounds

---

## Kala-azar (Visceral Leishmaniasis) {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

**Agent:** *Leishmania donovani*, a protozoan parasite. **Vector:**
the **sandfly** (*Phlebotomus* species) — a different vector family
entirely from the mosquito-borne diseases covered so far in this
curriculum.

**Geographic distribution:** historically concentrated in **Bihar and
neighbouring eastern states**, making it one of India's most
geographically clustered vector-borne diseases.

**Clinical features:** prolonged fever, **hepatosplenomegaly**,
progressive anaemia, weight loss, and darkening of the skin (the name
"kala-azar" means "black fever"). **Post-Kala-azar Dermal Leishmaniasis
(PKDL)** can follow apparent cure, presenting as skin lesions and
serving as a continuing reservoir for transmission.

---

## Diagnosis, Treatment, and Elimination {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

- **Diagnosis:** the **rK39 rapid diagnostic test** — a simple,
  field-deployable antibody test that has greatly simplified case
  detection compared to older invasive splenic/bone-marrow aspirate
  methods
- **Treatment:** **single-dose liposomal amphotericin B** is now the
  preferred regimen — a major improvement over older, longer,
  more toxic regimens, improving both cure rates and treatment
  completion
- **National Kala-azar Elimination Programme target:** fewer than
  **1 case per 10,000 population** at the block level — the same
  "elimination as a public health problem" framing (a defined,
  measurable threshold) already seen for lymphatic filariasis and
  leprosy, rather than a claim of zero cases

---

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 1

Blood samples for diagnosing lymphatic filariasis are conventionally
collected at night because:

- The parasite is only viable in cold blood
- [Microfilariae show nocturnal periodicity, circulating in peripheral blood mainly at night]{.correct data-explanation="Microfilarial nocturnal periodicity is synchronized with the night-biting Culex vector, which is why diagnostic blood collection is timed to the night."}
- Daytime samples clot too quickly
- Patients are only available at night
:::

### Question 4

The National Kala-azar Elimination Programme defines "elimination" as:

- Zero cases nationally
- [Fewer than 1 case per 10,000 population at the block level]{.correct data-explanation="Like lymphatic filariasis and leprosy elimination targets, kala-azar elimination is defined as a measurable threshold (under 1 case per 10,000 population at block level), not literal zero cases."}
- A 50% reduction from baseline
- Zero deaths, regardless of case count
